disease_info: Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is characterized by persistent and excessive worry about multiple domains of life (e.g., work, health, finances, family) occurring more days than not for at least six months, and is difficult for the individual to control. The anxiety is accompanied by physical and cognitive manifestations such as feeling keyed up, fatigue, impaired concentration, irritability, muscle tension, and sleep disturbance, leading to clinically significant distress or functional impairment. The course is often chronic and fluctuating, with symptoms waxing and waning in response to stressors but a baseline tendency toward pervasive apprehension. It is distinguished from other anxiety disorders by its broad, free-floating worry (rather than discrete panic attacks, specific phobias, or circumscribed obsessions) and by the absence of prominent compulsive rituals or trauma-focused re-experiencing.

narrative.personality: Dario is a methodical, intellectually curious technologist who prides himself on craftsmanship and mentoring while juggling a wide range of creative hobbies.
narrative.stressor: About eight months ago, Dario was promoted into a lead role on a high-visibility cloud migration project with an aggressive timeline, just as his company began quietly hinting at future restructuring. Accustomed to controlling details in his code and personal projects, he found himself responsible for coordinating multiple teams, managing ambiguous requirements, and fielding late-night messages from stakeholders in different time zones, all while trying to remain the calm expert his junior colleagues expected. Over the next several months, he increasingly brought work home—mentally rehearsing failure scenarios, replaying small mistakes, and adding more side projects in an effort to stay "ahead," which began to crowd out the restorative routines that had previously helped him decompress. When he noticed that his constant mental preoccupation with potential problems was eroding his concentration, slowing his coding, and making him irritable and unavailable with his spouse, he agreed at her urging to seek psychiatric help.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I feel constantly keyed up, like I can’t ever switch my brain or body off.”

narrative.personality: John is a gentle, steady, and community-minded storyteller and artist who balances meticulous planning with a relaxed, curious outlook on life.
narrative.stressor: Roughly nine months ago, one of John’s closest lifelong friends from his storytelling circle died unexpectedly, following the earlier loss of his wife several years before. This most recent death seemed to rupture the sense of continuity and safety he had maintained through his routines of beach walks, painting, and organizing the annual art-and-food festival, making him acutely aware of his own aging, memory lapses, and physical vulnerability. Over the subsequent months, he found himself increasingly preoccupied with the idea that something bad might happen to his remaining family members or to himself, checking on them frequently and second-guessing his ability to keep up his commitments to the festival and oral history project. When his grown children noticed he was turning down social invitations, spending long evenings ruminating over "what if" scenarios instead of enjoying his usual music and painting, and voicing fears about becoming a burden, they encouraged him to talk with a psychiatrist.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I just can’t stop worrying about everything that could go wrong for me and my family.”

narrative.personality: Natalie is a driven, data-focused fundraiser with a competitive streak and a cautious, hyper-prepared style that extends from her campaigns to her time in the mountains.
narrative.stressor: About seven to eight months ago, Natalie’s teenage child began struggling academically and showing signs of depression, just as her organization launched a make-or-break capital campaign with ambitious targets tied to her performance. Used to managing pressure by over-preparing and outworking problems, she responded by tightening control at home—monitoring grades, researching treatments late into the night—while simultaneously taking on extra responsibilities at work to ensure the campaign’s success. Over the following months, the sense that she alone needed to anticipate every possible setback, both for her child’s wellbeing and for the campaign, expanded into a constant, background sense of being on alert; she found it harder to enjoy trail runs or focus on data analysis without her mind jumping to worst-case scenarios. When she began noticing that this continual internal "on switch" was undermining her decision-making at work, straining her marriage, and leaving her feeling unable to relax even during her beloved mountain outings, she sought psychiatric evaluation at the suggestion of a colleague who had noticed the change in her demeanor.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I feel on edge all the time, like I’m bracing for something bad to happen and can’t ever relax.”
